title: Bengal's Shakta and Vaishnava streams
hook: a clerk's account book fills up with songs to Kali

segments.voice: Yesterday, Bengal's Shakta and Vaishnava streams: a conch at dusk for the Goddess, and a drum in the next lane for Krishna. Which sound did you notice living beside another? Day one thousand three hundred seventy-seven.

An office in Calcutta. A young clerk is supposed to be copying figures into the account book. Rows of numbers, day after day. But the other clerks notice that the margins of his ledger are filling up with something else. Lines of verse. Songs. Songs to Kali, the dark Mother. Somebody takes the book to the employer, expecting the young man to be fired. The employer opens it, starts reading, and doesn't stop. Today, we follow the Shakta stream through one singer: Ramprasad Sen.
screen: `A CLERK AND HIS LEDGER.` → `SONGS IN THE MARGINS.` → `THE EMPLOYER READS.`

segments.voice: Tradition says the employer was so moved that, instead of dismissing him, he sent Ramprasad home to his village with an allowance, so he could do nothing but sing. And sing he did. His songs, the stories say, spread from village to village, sung by boatmen and farmers, and tradition gives a melody his name. Turn it once, and listen to how he talks to Kali. Not like a courtier bowing to a queen. Like a child to his mother. In one song, in paraphrase, he complains: other children have a mother who looks after them, so why am I left like this? Is this how a mother behaves? He sulks, he pleads, he threatens to tell everyone. That's the Shakta stream at its warmest. The Goddess may be fierce, with a sword and a necklace of heads, but to the singer she is Ma, and a child is allowed to be cross with his mother. Turn it again. There's a story people tell about him. He was mending a fence and needed someone to hold the rope on the other side. His young daughter came and held it. Later, when he thanked her, she said she'd been away the whole time. So who held the rope? In the story, the Mother herself, wearing a little girl's face. And once more. His songs aren't only sweet. In one, he scolds his own mind as a lazy farmer: this human life is a good field, he says, and you've left it lying fallow. Tend it, and gold would grow. Tender with the Mother, hard on himself. That's the voice that came out of an account book.
screen: `SONGS IN THE ACCOUNT BOOK` · `A CHILD, CROSS WITH HIS MOTHER` · `WHO HELD THE ROPE?` · `THE FIELD LEFT FALLOW`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: the field. Sit, and let the breath slow. Picture your day as a small plot of ground. Some of it is planted: things you tended, people you looked after. Some of it is lying fallow: a thing you keep meaning to start, a call you haven't made. Don't scold yourself. Just walk around the field in your mind and notice. Then choose one small patch you could plant tomorrow. If you pray, you can call on the Mother, or on God, as the one who holds the rope on the other side. The bell holds the time.
Bengal's Shakta and Vaishnava streams. Today, the Shakta stream in Ramprasad Sen, the clerk who filled his ledger with songs and talked to Kali like a child to his mother. Today's word.
screen: `BENGAL'S SHAKTA AND VAISHNAVA STREAMS — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: Bengal's Shakta and Vaishnava streams. Today, plant one small thing in the fallow patch you found, five minutes on the thing you keep putting off. Day one thousand three hundred seventy-seven.

howItsDone: Ramprasad's songs to Kali are sung in Bengal at Kali Puja, at home and in devotional gatherings, as part of the song tradition known as Shyama Sangeet.

pairs: held by the Mother, in the story

myth: in the story, Ramprasad is fired for writing songs at work

he complains, pleads and sulks, because she is Ma.

fork.setup: you're Ramprasad's employer. a clerk's ledger is full of songs to Kali instead of figures. what do you do?
options: send him home with an allowance to sing.
tell him to keep the songs at home.
fork.reveal: tradition says the employer read on, was moved, and gave him an allowance so he could do nothing but sing.

trapdoor: what you thought: devotion to a fierce goddess must be fearful.
what it means: Ramprasad talks to Kali like a child to his mother, cross, pleading, sure of her love.
what a scholar hears: his songs belong to Shyama Sangeet, songs to the dark Mother, and tradition names a melody, the Ramprasadi tune, after him.

sources.ref: Traditional accounts of Ramprasad Sen: the ledger, the allowance, the fence

notes: Editor pass: the fence story's garbled sentence ('when he went inside, his daughter said...') rewritten; 'a melody even took his name' softened to 'tradition gives a melody his name'.
The ledger story (employer often named as Durgacharan Mitra) and the allowance (in some tellings from Raja Krishnachandra of Nadia) are told as tradition; confirm the paraphrase.
The fence story: tradition says Kali, in the form of his daughter, helped him bind the fence. Confirm the version told (daughter absent; the Mother held the rope).

Song paraphrases: the complaint to the Mother (a child neglected), and 'mana tumi krishi kaj jano na' (O mind, you don't know how to farm; the field of human birth lies fallow; tend it and gold would grow). Confirm.
'Ramprasadi sur' as a named melody: confirm.
Kali's necklace of heads is mentioned only as iconography; confirm tone is respectful for Shakta listeners.
